title: Bernard on love
hook: we love ourselves, then God for ourselves, then God for God, and at last ourselves for God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cistercians, the white monks of Cîteaux. Your line was plainer. What did you let go of? Today, a Cistercian abbot writes about love. Day eight hundred two.

A small girl visits her grandmother because there are cookies. That's the honest truth of it. Years later, she still visits, but now it's for the grandmother: the stories, the laugh, the hands. Later still, long after the cookies stopped mattering, she notices something odd. The person she has become was shaped by those visits. Loving her grandmother changed how she loves herself. A monk wrote a whole ladder of love along those lines, except the one he was climbing toward was God. Today's word is his name: Bernard.
screen: `FIRST, THE COOKIES.` → `THEN, THE GRANDMOTHER.` → `A LADDER OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Start with the question. Bernard was a Cistercian abbot at a monastery called Clairvaux. Someone asked him why God should be loved, and how much. His answer opens his little book On Loving God: the reason for loving God is God, and the measure is to love without measure. Then he sets out a ladder. Next, the first two rungs. At first, Bernard says, we love ourselves, for our own sake. That's where people begin, and he doesn't scold it. Then trouble comes, and we turn to God for help. Now we love God, but still for our own sake, for what God gives. Bernard counts that as real love, a true step up. Then, the third rung. Keep coming back for help, he says, and something shifts. You begin to taste how good God is, and you love God not for what you get but because God is good. In the Douay-Rheims, the first letter of John puts the root of it plainly: "Let us therefore love God, because God first hath loved us." Finally, the top rung, the strangest. You love even yourself only for God's sake. Bernard isn't sure anyone fully reaches it in this life; he wonders aloud whether it waits for the next. Elsewhere, preaching on the Song of Songs, he says love needs no reward beyond itself: I love because I love. The ladder starts with need and ends there, with love that asks for nothing back. That's today's line: love for love's sake.
screen: `LOVE WITHOUT MEASURE.` · `FIRST FOR OURSELVES.` · `THEN GOD, FOR GOD'S SAKE.` · `AT LAST, OURSELVES FOR GOD.` · then, large: `LOVE FOR LOVE'S SAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love one thing for its own sake. For the sit, choose one thing you love: a person, a place, a piece of music, the light in a certain window. Hold it in mind. Notice how much of the love is about what it gives you. That's all right; Bernard starts there too. Then try, just for a moment, to love it simply because it's good. Not useful. Good. If you pray, you can let that turn toward God, who, the letter of John says, loved first. The bell holds the time.
Bernard. The Cistercian abbot whose ladder of love rises from loving ourselves to loving God for God's sake, and at last, ourselves for God. Today's word.
Your line: love for love's sake. Today, do one kind thing for someone that can't possibly come back to you. Don't mention it. Day eight hundred two.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Bernard of Clairvaux as a Doctor of the Church; his On Loving God and his sermons on the Song of Songs are read in monasteries and by people making retreats, and his feast is kept in late summer.

notes: On Loving God paraphrased: ch. 1 (the cause of loving God is God; the measure is to love without measure); chs. 8–10 (the four degrees; Bernard's doubt whether the fourth is fully reached in this life). The index hook gives three steps; the script names all four, as Bernard does, and the hook field is adjusted to match. Confirm.
Sermon 83 on the Song of Songs paraphrased ('I love because I love'); confirm reference.
The grandmother image is the script's own illustration, not Bernard's; confirm it doesn't trivialize. Bernard's own image (servant, hireling, son) could replace it.
